note.explanation: Data are raw facts gathered about things. We can classify data as qualitative or quantitative, collect it using methods such as surveys, organise it in tables and charts, and use visualizations to understand it. Good data gathering starts by understanding the problem.
examples: Favourite ice cream flavour is qualitative data; number of students is quantitative, discrete data.
Students' heights are continuous data because they can take measured values within a range.
note.checkAnswer: The number of students is discrete data because it is countable and takes separate whole-number values.
note.simple: Data are facts. Sort and display them clearly so you can understand them and answer questions.
note.checkQuestion: What type of data is the number of students in a class, and why?
note.title: Gathering and understanding data
steps: Understand the problem and decide what information is needed.
Choose a suitable method, such as a survey, to collect the data.
Organise the information in tables or charts.
Analyse and display the data to find patterns and communicate results.
note.answer: Data are raw facts gathered about things.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.1. What is data?
(a) Processed information (b) Raw facts gathered about things (c) A collection of numbers only (d) A list of observed events
rationales: This is not the definition of data; processed information is information produced from data.
This is correct: data are raw facts gathered about things.
Data are not limited to numbers; they can also be words, categories, or observations.
Observed events can provide data, but this is not the general definition.

options: Number of students in a class
mcqs.stem:
Q9.2. Which of the following is an example of qualitative data?
(a) Temperature readings in degrees Celsius (b) Number of students in a class (c) Favourite ice cream flavours (d) Test scores out of 100
rationales: Temperature readings are numerical measurements, so they are quantitative.
A number of students is a count, so it is quantitative discrete data.
This is correct: flavour names describe categories, not numerical amounts.
Test scores are numerical, so they are quantitative.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.3. What type of data involves distinct, separate values that are countable?
(a) Nominal Data (b) Ordinal Data (c) Discrete Data (d) Continuous Data
rationales: Nominal data name categories without an order; they are not defined as countable numerical values.
Ordinal data are categories with an order, not distinct countable numerical values.
This is correct: discrete data consist of distinct, separate, countable values.
Continuous data can take measured values throughout a range, rather than only separate countable values.

options: Number of cars in a parking lot
mcqs.stem:
Q9.4. What is an example of continuous data?
(a) Number of cars in a parking lot (b) Height of students in centimetres (c) Types of fruits (d) Shirt sizes (small, medium, large)
rationales: Cars are counted in separate whole-number amounts, so this is discrete data.
This is correct: height is measured and can take values within a range.
Fruit types are categories, not continuous measurements.
These are ordered categories, not continuous measurements.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.5. What type of data is used to categorize items without implying any order?
(a) Ordinal Data (b) Discrete Data (c) Nominal Data (d) Continuous Data
rationales: Ordinal data have categories that can be placed in an order.
Discrete data are countable numerical values, not unordered categories.
This is correct: nominal data categorize items without implying any order.
Continuous data are measurements that can take values within a range.

options: By writing it in long paragraphs
By creating tables, charts, and graphs
By storing it in random files
By keeping it in a messy notebook
mcqs.stem:
Q9.6. How can you organise data to make it easier to analyse?
(a) By writing it in long paragraphs (b) By creating tables, charts, and graphs (c) By storing it in random files (d) By keeping it in a messy notebook
rationales: Long paragraphs make comparisons and patterns harder to find.
This is correct: tables, charts, and graphs organise data for easier analysis.
Random files make data difficult to find and compare.
A messy notebook does not organise information for analysis.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.7. Which tool can be used to create surveys online?
(a) Microsoft Word (b) Google Forms
(c) Excel Spreadsheets (d) Adobe Photoshop
rationales: Word is mainly used for creating documents, not online surveys.
This is correct: Google Forms can be used to create online surveys.
Spreadsheets can organise data, but are not the survey-creation tool identified here.
Photoshop is an image-editing tool, not an online survey tool.

options: To gather information to answer questions or make decisions
mcqs.stem:
Q9.8. What is the main purpose of data collection?
(a) To create random numbers
(b) To gather information to answer questions or make decisions
(c) To delete old data
(d) To format text documents
rationales: Creating random numbers is not the main purpose of data collection.
This is correct: data are gathered to answer questions or support decisions.
Deleting old data is not the purpose of collecting data.
Formatting documents is unrelated to the main purpose of data collection.

options: To make data easier to understand by turning it into pictures
mcqs.stem:
Q9.9. What is the primary purpose of data visualization?
(a) To generate random numbers (b) To convert text into data
(c) To make data easier to understand by turning it into pictures
(d) To hide complex data
rationales: Generating random numbers is not data visualization.
Visualization displays data; it does not convert text into data.
This is correct: visualizations use pictures such as charts and graphs to make data easier to understand.
Visualization is used to clarify data, not hide it.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.10. Which tool is specifically designed for creating detailed and interactive visualizations?
(a) Microsoft Excel (b) Google Sheets
(c) Tableau (d) PowerPoint
rationales: Excel can create charts, but it is not the tool identified as specifically designed for detailed, interactive visualizations.
Google Sheets can make charts, but it is not the tool identified here for detailed, interactive visualizations.
This is correct: Tableau is specifically designed for detailed and interactive visualizations.
PowerPoint is presentation software, rather than the tool identified for interactive visualizations.

mcqs.stem:
Q9.11. What is the first step in the data science process?
(a) Data Cleaning (b) Data Analysis
(c) Data Collection (d) Understanding the problem
rationales: Data cleaning is done after data have been collected.
Data analysis takes place after the problem and data have been understood.
Collection follows deciding what problem needs to be solved and what data are needed.
This is correct: first understand the problem.

options: The speed at which data is generated
The different forms data can take
The sheer amount of data being collected
mcqs.stem:
Q9.12. What does the 'Volume' characteristic of Big Data refer to?
(a) The speed at which data is generated
(b) The different forms data can take
(c) The sheer amount of data being collected
(d) The way data is processed
rationales: Speed of generation refers to the rate of data, not its volume.
Different forms refer to variety, not volume.
This is correct: volume is the sheer amount of data collected.
Processing method is not the meaning of volume.

options: An unusual or extreme value that doesn't fit the pattern
The middle value when all values are arranged in order
mcqs.stem:
Q9.13. What is an outlier in a dataset?
(a) The most frequent value
(b) The average of all values
(c) An unusual or extreme value that doesn't fit the pattern
(d) The middle value when all values are arranged in order
rationales: The most frequent value is the mode, not an outlier.
The average is the mean, not an outlier.
This is correct: an outlier is an unusual or extreme value that does not fit the pattern.
The middle value is the median, not an outlier.

options: It converts data into a code to prevent unauthorized access.
It makes data available to everyone online.
mcqs.stem:
Q9.14. What does data encryption do?
(a) It converts data into a code to prevent unauthorized access.
(b) It makes data available to everyone online.
(c) It automatically deletes old data.
(d) It speeds up internet connection.
rationales: This is correct: encryption codes data to prevent unauthorized access.
Encryption protects data; it does not make it available to everyone.
Encryption does not automatically delete old data.
Encryption does not speed up an internet connection.

written.text: Q9.1. What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative data?
written.finalAnswer: Qualitative data describe qualities or categories; quantitative data are numerical and can be counted or measured.

rubric.why: This distinguishes data that describe categories or qualities.
rubric.how: Say that they describe qualities or categories.

rubric.why: This identifies quantitative data as numerical.
rubric.how: Say they are numerical and can be counted or measured.

modelAnswer: Qualitative data describe qualities or categories.
Quantitative data are numerical and can be counted or measured.

written.text: Q9.2. Give an example of continuous data and explain why it is considered continuous.
written.finalAnswer: A student's height is continuous data because it is measured and can take values within a range.

rubric.why: A suitable measured quantity demonstrates continuous data.
rubric.description: Give an example of continuous data.
rubric.how: Name a measurement such as height, temperature, or weight.

rubric.why: The reason shows understanding that continuous values can vary across a range.
rubric.description: Explain why the example is continuous.
rubric.how: State that it is measured and can take values within a range.

modelAnswer: A student's height is an example of continuous data.
It is measured and can take values within a range.

written.text: Q9.3. Which method would you use to collect opinions from a large group of people about a new school policy?
written.finalAnswer: I would use a survey, such as an online survey made with Google Forms.

rubric.why: A survey is a suitable way to collect opinions from many people.
rubric.how: Choose a survey or questionnaire.

rubric.why: Connecting the method to a large group or online tool explains its suitability.
rubric.description: Explain or specify how the method will be used.
rubric.how: Mention reaching many people or using an online survey tool.

modelAnswer: I would use a survey to collect the opinions.
An online survey, such as one made with Google Forms, can be sent to many people.

written.text: Q9.4. What type of data is the number of students in your class?
written.finalAnswer: Discrete quantitative data.

rubric.why: The number of students is a count of separate values.
rubric.description: Identify the data type as discrete.
rubric.how: Write discrete.

rubric.why: The number is also numerical and countable.
rubric.description: Identify its numerical or countable nature.
rubric.how: Write quantitative or explain that it is countable.

modelAnswer: The number of students is discrete quantitative data because it is countable.

written.text: Q9.5. Why is it important to organise data into tables or charts before analyzing it?
written.finalAnswer: Tables and charts make data easier to read, compare, and analyse, helping patterns to be identified.

rubric.why: Organisation makes information more manageable for analysis.
rubric.description: Explain how tables or charts help handle data.
rubric.how: Say they make data easier to read, compare, or analyse.

rubric.why: Finding patterns or trends is a key purpose of arranging data.
rubric.description: State what organised data help reveal.
rubric.how: Mention identifying patterns, trends, or understanding the data.

modelAnswer: Tables and charts organise data so it is easier to read, compare, and analyse.
They help us identify patterns and understand the information.

written.text: Q9.6. What is one advantage of using online tools like Google Forms for collecting survey data?
written.finalAnswer: Google Forms makes it easy to collect responses from many people online and organise them for analysis.

rubric.why: An advantage should identify a practical benefit of online collection.
rubric.description: Give one benefit of collecting responses online.
rubric.how: Mention reaching many respondents or collecting responses easily.

rubric.why: A further benefit explains how the tool helps manage the collected data.
rubric.how: Mention organising results, analysis, or saving time.

modelAnswer: Google Forms makes it easy to collect survey responses from many people online.
It can also organise responses for analysis.

written.text: Q9.7. Why might you need to integrate data from different sources when working on a project?
written.finalAnswer: Integrating data from different sources gives a more complete view and combines information needed to answer the project's question.

rubric.why: Integration means bringing together relevant information from separate sources.
rubric.how: Say it combines data from different sources.

rubric.why: The combined information can make the project findings more useful.
rubric.description: Explain why the combined data are useful.
rubric.how: Mention a more complete view or better answers to the project question.

modelAnswer: A project may need information held in different sources, so the data must be combined.
Integrating them gives a more complete view and helps answer the project's question.

written.text: Q9.8. Describe a scenario where discrete data might be more useful than continuous data.
written.finalAnswer: To track attendance, count the number of students present each day; these separate counts are discrete data.

rubric.why: A scenario involving a count is appropriate for discrete data.
rubric.how: For example, count students present or books borrowed.

rubric.why: The explanation must connect the count to distinct, countable values.
rubric.description: Explain why discrete data fit the scenario.
rubric.how: Say the values are separate, countable, or whole-number counts.

modelAnswer: A school could count the number of students present each day to track attendance.
These are discrete data because the students are counted in separate whole-number values.

written.text: Q9.9. Explain why data visualization is important. How does it help in understanding complex information?
written.finalAnswer: Data visualization presents data as pictures such as charts and graphs, making complex information easier to understand and helping reveal patterns.

rubric.why: This states how visualization presents data.
rubric.how: Mention pictures, charts, or graphs.

rubric.why: This gives the benefit for understanding complex information.
rubric.how: Say it makes information easier to understand or reveals patterns.

modelAnswer: Data visualization presents data as pictures, such as charts and graphs.
It makes complex information easier to understand and helps reveal patterns.

written.text: Q9.10. Describe what a line graph is used for and provide an example of data that could be displayed using a line graph.
written.finalAnswer: A line graph shows how data change, often over time; it could display the daily temperature during a week.

rubric.why: A line graph is useful for showing change or a trend.
rubric.description: State what a line graph shows.
rubric.how: Mention change or trends, often over time.

rubric.why: A relevant example shows how the graph can be applied.
rubric.description: Give suitable data for a line graph.
rubric.how: Give a measured value tracked over time, such as daily temperature.

modelAnswer: A line graph is used to show how data change, often over time.
For example, it could show the daily temperature during a week.

written.text: Q9.11. Explain the use of scatter plots in visualizing continuous data. Provide an example of a situation where a scatter plot would be useful.
written.finalAnswer: A scatter plot displays pairs of continuous values as points and helps show a relationship between them; it could compare students' height and arm span.

rubric.why: This explains how a scatter plot represents paired values and can reveal relationships.
rubric.description: Describe the use of a scatter plot.
rubric.how: Say it plots paired values as points to show a possible relationship.

rubric.why: A paired-variable example demonstrates an appropriate use.
rubric.how: Name two continuous quantities that could be compared.

modelAnswer: A scatter plot displays pairs of continuous values as points and can show a relationship between them.
For example, it could compare students' height and arm span.

written.text: Q9.1. Explain the differences between qualitative and quantitative data. Provide examples of each type.
written.finalAnswer: Qualitative data describe qualities or categories, such as favourite ice cream flavours. Quantitative data are numerical and can be counted or measured, such as number of students or students' heights.

rubric.why: A clear definition distinguishes non-numerical descriptions from quantities.
rubric.how: Explain that they describe qualities or categories.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates qualitative data.
rubric.description: Give an example of qualitative data.
rubric.how: Name a category such as favourite flavour or colour.

rubric.why: A clear definition identifies quantitative data as numbers.
rubric.how: State that these data are numerical and counted or measured.

rubric.why: Suitable numerical examples complete the comparison.
rubric.description: Give an example and make the contrast clear.
rubric.how: Use counts or measurements, and distinguish them from categories.

modelAnswer: Qualitative data describe qualities or categories rather than numerical amounts.
For example, students' favourite ice cream flavours are qualitative data.
Quantitative data are numerical and can be counted or measured.
For example, the number of students is a count, while students' heights are measurements.

written.text: Q9.2. Describe the process of conducting a survey to gather data about students' favourite extracurricular activities.
written.finalAnswer: Decide the survey question, list suitable activity choices, select students to ask, collect responses using a survey, organise and analyse the results, and present the findings in a table or chart.

rubric.why: A clear purpose ensures the survey collects relevant data.
rubric.how: State that the question should ask about favourite extracurricular activities.

rubric.why: Appropriate choices and respondents make the survey usable.
rubric.description: Set up the response options and respondents.
rubric.how: List activities and decide which students will be surveyed.

rubric.why: The survey method is the means of gathering the data.
rubric.how: Use a survey, such as Google Forms, and gather students' answers.

rubric.why: Organising and presenting results makes them understandable.
rubric.how: Count responses, analyse them, and display them in a table or chart.

modelAnswer: First, decide that the survey will find students' favourite extracurricular activities.
Write a clear question and provide suitable activity choices, such as sports, music, and clubs.
Choose the students to survey and collect their responses using a survey, such as Google Forms.
Count and organise the responses, analyse which activities are most popular, and present the findings in a table or chart.

written.text: Q9.3. Compare and contrast continuous and discrete data. Use examples to show how each type of data might be used in a school setting, such as in measuring student performance or tracking attendance.
written.finalAnswer: Discrete data have separate, countable values, such as the number of students present. Continuous data are measured and can take values within a range, such as students' heights or time taken to complete a test.

rubric.why: The definition identifies the defining feature of discrete data.
rubric.how: State that values are distinct, separate, and countable.

rubric.why: A school-based count illustrates discrete data.
rubric.description: Give and explain a discrete school example.
rubric.how: Use a count such as students present in class.

rubric.why: The definition distinguishes measured values that vary across a range.
rubric.how: State that they are measured and can take values within a range.

rubric.why: A school-related measurement demonstrates continuous data.
rubric.description: Give and explain a continuous school example.
rubric.how: Use a measurement such as height or time taken for a test.

modelAnswer: Discrete data consist of distinct, separate values that are countable.
For example, a school can count how many students are present each day; the result is a whole-number count.
Continuous data are measured and can take values within a range.
For example, students' heights or the time taken to complete a test can be measured and may include values between whole numbers.

written.text: Q9.4. Analyse the benefits and challenges of using digital tools like Google Forms for data collection.
written.finalAnswer: Google Forms can collect responses online from many people, save time, and organise results for analysis. Challenges include limited access to devices or the internet, unclear or biased questions, incomplete responses, and the need to protect respondents' information.

rubric.why: Online reach is a central benefit of digital collection.
rubric.description: Explain a benefit related to collecting responses.
rubric.how: Mention collecting responses online or reaching many people.

rubric.why: Efficient organisation and handling are additional benefits.
rubric.how: Mention saving time or organising results for analysis.

rubric.why: Practical access issues can prevent complete participation.
rubric.how: Mention lack of internet or devices, or incomplete responses.

rubric.why: Good analysis considers the quality and protection of collected data.
rubric.how: Mention privacy or poorly worded questions that affect results.

modelAnswer: Google Forms can collect responses online from many people and can save time.
It can organise responses so that they are easier to analyse.
However, some students may not have access to the internet or a suitable device, and some may leave questions unanswered.
Questions must be clear and unbiased, and respondents' information should be protected.

written.text: Q9.5. Imagine you are tasked with organizing a school event and need to collect data on students' preferences for activities and refreshments.
written.finalAnswer: Use a survey to ask students to choose preferred activities and refreshments; organise and analyse the responses in tables or charts to help plan the event.

rubric.why: A suitable collection method is needed to gather preferences.
rubric.how: Use a survey or online questionnaire.

rubric.why: The survey must cover both parts of the event preferences.
rubric.how: Ask about preferred activities and refreshments.

rubric.why: Clear response options and gathering student answers make the data useful.
rubric.description: Describe how to obtain usable responses.
rubric.how: Offer choices and collect responses from students.

rubric.why: Organised results support the event-planning decision.
rubric.description: Explain how to use the data.
rubric.how: Summarise responses in a table or chart and use them to plan.

modelAnswer: I would create a survey asking students which activities and refreshments they prefer.
I would provide clear choices and collect responses from the students, using an online tool such as Google Forms if suitable.
I would organise and count the responses in a table.
I would use a chart to compare the preferences and choose activities and refreshments for the event.

written.text: Q9.6. Explain the role of tables and charts in data analysis. Provide an example of how you could use a table or chart to present data about students' grades in different subjects.
written.finalAnswer: Tables organise data in rows and columns, while charts show comparisons or patterns visually. A table or bar chart could show students' grades in subjects such as English, Mathematics, and Science.

rubric.why: Tables arrange data so values can be found and compared.
rubric.how: Say tables organise data in rows and columns for comparison.

rubric.why: Charts make patterns or comparisons easier to see.
rubric.how: State that charts display data visually and help show patterns.

rubric.why: The example must use the requested subject-grade data.
rubric.how: Use student grades across different subjects.

rubric.why: A suitable display and its use show how the data can be presented.
rubric.description: Explain how the example would be displayed.
rubric.how: Use a table or bar chart to compare grades by subject.

modelAnswer: A table organises data in rows and columns so that values can be found and compared.
A chart displays data visually and can make patterns or differences easier to see.
For example, I could list students' grades in English, Mathematics, and Science in a table.
A bar chart could then compare the grades across subjects.

written.text: Q9.7. Describe a situation where non-numeric data is essential. How would you collect, store, and analyse this type of data? Discuss the tools and techniques you would use to ensure the data is accurately interpreted.
written.finalAnswer: To understand students' reasons for choosing a school club, collect written survey answers or interview responses. Store answers in labelled categories or a spreadsheet, group similar responses, and check the original answers so that their meaning is interpreted accurately.

rubric.why: A relevant situation demonstrates why descriptions or opinions matter.
rubric.description: Give a situation requiring non-numeric data.
rubric.how: Use opinions, explanations, or reasons that cannot be captured by numbers alone.

rubric.why: A suitable method is needed to gather descriptive information.
rubric.description: Explain how to collect the data.
rubric.how: Use written survey answers, interviews, or observations.

rubric.why: Organised storage makes qualitative responses manageable.
rubric.description: Explain how to store the data.
rubric.how: Store responses in a labelled spreadsheet or organised categories.

rubric.why: Careful coding and checking reduce inaccurate interpretation.
rubric.how: Group similar answers and check categories against the original responses.

modelAnswer: Non-numeric data are essential when a school wants to understand why students prefer particular clubs.
The school could collect written answers in a survey or ask students in interviews.
Responses could be stored in a spreadsheet with clear labels, or grouped into categories such as sport, creativity, and friendship.
The answers could be analysed by grouping similar ideas and counting how often they occur, while checking the original responses so their meanings are not misinterpreted.

written.text: Q9.8. Explain the concept of data visualization. How does it help in understanding complex data? Provide examples of different types of visualizations and their applications in real-life scenarios.
written.finalAnswer: Data visualization presents data as pictures, such as charts and graphs. It makes complex information easier to understand and helps reveal patterns and comparisons. Line graphs can show changes over time, and scatter plots can show relationships between two continuous variables.

rubric.why: A definition explains that visualization represents data visually.
rubric.how: Say data are presented as pictures, charts, or graphs.

rubric.why: This explains how visualization helps with complex information.
rubric.how: Mention clearer understanding, patterns, or comparisons.

rubric.why: A visualization and relevant use demonstrate application.
rubric.how: For example, use a line graph to display temperature or sales over time.

rubric.why: A second type and its purpose demonstrate further understanding.
rubric.how: Explain that a scatter plot can show the relationship between two continuous variables.

modelAnswer: Data visualization is the presentation of data as pictures, such as charts and graphs.
It makes complex information easier to understand and helps people see patterns and comparisons.
A line graph can show change over time, such as daily temperature or a business's sales each month.
A scatter plot displays paired values as points and can show a relationship, such as the relationship between study time and test scores.

written.text: Q9.9. Discuss the importance and benefits of data visualization. Why is it essential for businesses and decision-makers to use charts, graphs, and dashboards?
written.finalAnswer: Visualizations make data easier to understand, reveal patterns and comparisons, and communicate findings quickly. Businesses and decision-makers can use charts, graphs, and dashboards to monitor results, identify problems, and make informed decisions.

rubric.why: Clear communication is a main benefit of visual representation.
rubric.how: Say they present information clearly and quickly.

rubric.why: Finding patterns and comparisons supports analysis.
rubric.how: Mention patterns, trends, or comparisons.

rubric.why: The answer should connect visualizations to their users and tools.
rubric.description: Explain their relevance to businesses and decision-makers.
rubric.how: Mention business use of charts, graphs, or dashboards.

rubric.why: The value of visualization lies in supporting action and decisions.
rubric.how: Explain that they help monitor results, spot problems, or make informed decisions.

modelAnswer: Data visualization makes information easier to understand and communicate.
Charts and graphs help people identify patterns, trends, and comparisons in data.
Businesses and decision-makers can use dashboards to view important information together and monitor results.
This helps them spot problems and make informed decisions.

written.text: Q9.10. Differentiate between nominal, ordinal, discrete, and continuous data. For each type, describe a suitable visualization technique and provide a specific example of how this technique can be used to represent that type of data effectively.
written.finalAnswer: Nominal data are unordered categories, such as favourite fruit, and can be shown in a bar chart. Ordinal data are ordered categories, such as satisfaction levels, and can be shown in an ordered bar chart. Discrete data are separate countable values, such as books borrowed, and can be shown in a bar chart. Continuous data are measurements across a range, such as height, and can be shown in a histogram.

rubric.why: Nominal data must be distinguished as categories without an order.
rubric.description: Define nominal data and give an appropriate display or example.
rubric.how: State unordered categories and use an example such as fruit type.

rubric.why: Ordinal data are distinguished by the order of their categories.
rubric.description: Define ordinal data and give an appropriate display or example.
rubric.how: State that categories have an order, such as satisfaction levels.

rubric.why: Discrete values are separate and countable, unlike continuous measurements.
rubric.description: Define discrete data and give an appropriate display or example.
rubric.how: Use a count such as books borrowed and mention a bar chart.

rubric.why: Continuous data are measurements that can vary within a range.
rubric.description: Define continuous data and give an appropriate display or example.
rubric.how: Use a measurement such as height and mention a suitable graph.

modelAnswer: Nominal data are categories with no implied order; for example, favourite fruit can be represented in a bar chart.
Ordinal data are categories with an order; for example, satisfaction levels can be shown in an ordered bar chart.
Discrete data have separate, countable values; for example, the number of books borrowed can be shown in a bar chart.
Continuous data are measured values that can take values within a range; for example, students' heights can be represented in a histogram.

examTips: Short questions usually ask for a definition, a suitable example, or a reason. Give the definition and connect your example to it.
Long questions often ask you to compare data types or describe a collection-and-analysis process. Write in clear steps and include examples.
For data-type questions, explain the key difference: categories, ordered categories, countable values, or measured values.
For survey questions, include the question, respondents, collection method, organisation of responses, and how the results will be used.
For visualization questions, name the chart or graph and state what it helps show.

example.answer: First, decide that the survey will find students' favourite extracurricular activities. Write a clear question and provide suitable activity choices, such as sports, music, and clubs. Choose the students to survey and collect their responses using a survey, such as Google Forms. Count and organise the responses, analyse which activities are most popular, and present the findings in a table or chart.

explain.title: Data and its kinds
explain.body: Data are raw facts gathered about things. Qualitative data describe qualities or categories, while quantitative data are numerical and can be counted or measured.

explain.title: Four useful data types
explain.body: Nominal data are categories without an order. Ordinal data are ordered categories. Discrete data have separate, countable values. Continuous data are measurements that can take values within a range.

explain.title: Collecting and organising data
explain.body: First understand the problem and decide what information is needed. Then choose a collection method, such as a survey. Tables and charts organise information so it is easier to compare and analyse.

explain.title: Visualizing data
explain.body: Data visualization presents data as pictures such as charts and graphs. It helps people understand complex information, compare values, and notice patterns. A line graph can show change over time; a scatter plot can show a relationship between two values.

explain.title: Using data carefully
explain.body: Digital tools such as Google Forms can make collection and organisation easier, but check that questions are clear, responses are complete, and private information is protected. An outlier is an unusual or extreme value that does not fit the pattern.

mistakes: Do not call every numerical value continuous: a count such as the number of students is discrete.
Do not confuse nominal categories, which have no order, with ordinal categories, which do.
Do not give an example without explaining why it fits the data type.
For a survey process, do not stop at collecting answers; explain how you will organise and analyse them.
Do not say visualization hides data; it makes information easier to understand.
When discussing digital collection, consider both benefits and challenges, including access and privacy.
